title: Automatic quantification of myocardial remodeling features in human ventricular tissue from label-free microscopy
protocol: Collect left ventricular tissue samples from donors immediately after being placed on cardiopulmonary bypass.
Store the tissue samples in ice-cold Tyrode’s solution for transportation to the laboratory.
Transfer the tissue samples to a 1.5 mL tube containing ice-cold fixative solution of 4% paraformaldehyde.
Incubate the samples in the fixative solution for 1 hour at 4°C or on ice.
Remove the fixative solution and transfer the samples to 0.01% sodium azide-PBS at 4°C until embedded in paraffin blocks.
Carry out tissue dehydration and paraffin embedding with the Tissue-Tek Xpress x50 Tissue Processor System (Henry Schein, USA).
Mount tissue blocks using the paraffin embedding station EG1150H (Leica, Germany) and the HI1210 Water bath for paraffin sections (Leica, Germany).
Section tissue blocks with the microtome Shandon finesse 325 (Thermo Scientific, USA) to obtain 5-μm sections.
Mount the sections on microscope slides.
Allow the sections to dry for 24 hours before image acquisition.
Rotate a suitable objective lens into the imaging position.
Place the sample on the microscope sample holder.
Locate the sample using transmission or fluorescence imaging.
Focus the sample using transmission or fluorescence imaging.
Create a suitable light path to steer the femtosecond pulsed laser light to the sample.
Activate three detectors to simultaneously detect the SHG signal, cellular autofluorescence and lipofuscin autofluorescence.
Adjust each detector channel to detect the optimal wavelength range: SHG signal (380–420 nm).
Adjust each detector channel to detect the optimal wavelength range: Cellular autofluorescence (500–552 nm).
Adjust each detector channel to detect the optimal wavelength range: Lipofuscin autofluorescence (650–735 nm).
Tune the femtosecond pulsed laser to a central wavelength of 810 nm.
Adjust the transmission through the acousto-optic modulator so that ∼80 mW average power is focused on the sample through a plan-apochromat 20× objective (NA 0.8).
Adjust the acquisition parameters to acquire images with sufficient resolution and dynamic range.
Use a bit depth of 16 bits for image acquisition.
Acquire images at a zoom factor of 1.3 to ensure homogeneous illumination.
Capture images with dimensions of 1872 by 1872 pixels, resulting in a square pixel size of 170 nm by 170 nm.
Fully open the pinhole(s) for each channel during acquisition.
Optimize the detection of each detector channel by adjusting the detector gain and offset.
Use a range indicator lookup table while optimizing the detector settings to minimize data clipping.
Set Ch1 detector gain to 750, digital offset to 256.
Set ChS1 detector gain to 680, digital offset to 64.
Set Ch2 detector gain to 750, digital offset to 256.
Define a tilescan or mosaic image for samples larger than a single field-of-view.
Use a rectangular grid for rectangular/square samples.
Use a bounding box for irregular samples.
Ensure sufficient overlap (10%) between the different tiles.
Maintain microscope acquisition settings between independent sessions.
Select conventional internal detectors in a confocal NLO microscope setup.
Acquire all three channels simultaneously to ensure good lateral and axial overlap.
Fully open the pinhole for maximum signal.
Perform optical sectioning by selective two-photon excitation process.
Export 16-bit TIFF grayscale images from the original czi files using Zen Blue software.
Ensure each channel is detected in a separate file during export.
Use batch processing to export all images at once.
Copy image parameters for the first image using Export image parameters > Copy parameters.
Paste copied parameters into other images to maintain consistent settings.
Open three individual channels of each tissue section with ImageJ software.
Delimit the tissue of interest in every channel using the “Polygon selection” tool.
Select “Edit > Clear outside” to clean isolated regions that should be discarded from analysis.
Select “Image > Adjust > Brightness/Contrast” for automatic brightness scaling.
Press “Auto” once and then “Apply” for each channel image.
Save each adjusted image as a new 8-bit TIFF file.
Load each saved 8-bit TIFF file.
Split each loaded image into its individual grayscale channels.
Apply a binarization filter to the gray-level images corresponding to the SHG signal.
Generate binary masks for each of the SHG signal.
Apply a binarization filter to the gray-level images corresponding to the autofluorescence signal from the myocardial tissue.
Generate binary masks for the autofluorescence signal.
Use imbinarize function with threshold values in the range 0.17–0.35 for the autofluorescence signal.
Use imbinarize function with threshold values in the range 0.08–0.35 for the SHG signal.
Fill empty spaces less than 20 pixels in the myocardial tissue mask.
Identify and remove isolated segments and/or artifacts in the SHG binary mask.
Discard areas with less than 15 pixels in the SHG binary mask.
Separate the myosin and collagen signals in the SHG signal by considering that collagen is the part of the SHG signal that does not colocalize with the myocardial tissue mask.
Calculate a relative clustering degree as the product of percentages of collagen and clustering degree, which is expressed as per ten thousand (‱).
Divide the collagen binary mask into subimages of 500 × 500 pixels.
Include only subimages with a minimum of 200 activated pixels in the analysis.
Compute the collage clustering degree for each subimage.
Build the histogram of the collagen clustering degree from all subimages of a given image.
Determine the collagen clustering median as the median of the clustering distribution statistical distribution.
Calculate the collagen clustering dispersion as the interquartile range of the clustering degree statistical distribution.
Apply a binarization filter to the gray-level image corresponding to the lipofuscin signal to generate a binary lipofuscin mask.
Compute the percentage of lipofuscin as the number of activated pixels in the lipofuscin mask divided by the activated pixels in the myocardial tissue mask, then multiply by 100.
